10844-a-gentleman-from-mississippi:
A Gentleman from Mississippi, a novel founded on the popular play produced by William A. Brady and Joseph R. Grismer, tells of a senator from the South in the North. Illustrations show the senator with Bud Haines, the Langdon family at tea, and a defiant speech: after he has finished, he dares any man to deny a word. The introduction calls it a battle of right against wrong.

Honesty faces corruption, simplicity faces bribery and intrigue, in a story the author calls the story of today in America. The novel's politics are plain and earnest. Readers get a Progressive-era drama of reform, novelized from a stage hit.
15888-the-unwritten-literature-of-the-ho:
A study of Hopi oral literature by Hattie Greene Lockett, issued as Social Science Bulletin number two by the University of Arizona at Tucson in 1933. Lockett treats myth as a living force, not a dead tale. Her bulletin joins field notes to a general theory of myth in early life. The work serves students of Native America and of folklore.

Chapters survey Hopi country and people, social order, clan and marriage, and women's and men's work. Pottery and basket making, with their symbolism, and house building follow. Myth and folktale get full discussion, with notes on stability and intrusion. The bulletin still gives a clear, respectful entry to Hopi story life.
245-life-on-the-mississippi:
Mark Twain learned the Mississippi as a cub pilot and never forgot its lessons. Life on the Mississippi mixes river history, tall talk, and a return voyage down the great stream. Early chapters trace De Soto, La Salle, and the commerce of rafts and coal fleets.

Twain recalls pilot training, river lore, and the steamboat age with humor and regret. Later chapters visit changed towns and note what railroads took away. The book blends memoir, travel, and history in Twain's voice. It remains the great American river book. Twain's river memoir influenced travel writing long after steamboats faded.
2575-confessions-of-an-inquiring-spirit-:
In these confessions Samuel Taylor Coleridge inquires frankly into faith, reason, and the reading of Scripture. The 1892 Cassell edition pairs them with miscellaneous essays drawn from his journal The Friend. Coleridge was born in 1772, the youngest son of a Devon vicar, and his mind ranged across poetry, philosophy, and theology.

The confessions ask how a thinking person can hold both honest doubt and sincere belief, and the added essays touch morals, politics, and the life of the mind. Coleridge writes in rich, searching prose that rewards slow reading. The book suits readers who want a poet's wrestle with faith, not a catechism.
5769-the-shagganappi:
Pauline Johnson, known as Tekahionwake, gathers Indigenous stories in The Shagganappi, with an introduction by Ernest Thompson Seton and a dedication to the Boy Scouts. Seton recalls meeting Tekahionwake as an ideal type of her people, lithe and active, with clean-cut features, and his introduction frames her as a storyteller speaking across cultures. The tales that follow draw on Mohawk and wider Indigenous tradition.

Readers meet heroes, tricksters, and lessons carried in story form, told with Johnson's gift for vivid scene and moral clarity. The book suits young readers and families, and it holds historic interest as an early Indigenous author's work reaching a wide audience. Modern readers can value Johnson's voice while noting the period framing around it, which speaks of its time.
6958-frank-on-the-lower-mississippi:
Harry Castlemon sends Frank to the lower Mississippi just after Vicksburg has fallen and the army has marched into the city. Frank longs to see inside the rebel stronghold that so long held off fleet and army, and he leans on a great gun that spoke often at his bidding. The chapters promise a new paymaster, a night expedition, Archie in a predicament, and a mark for the Union.

A run for life, detective work, a first command, an unlucky flight, and a trip up the Washita carry the tale onward. Rival spies, a scouting party, Tom the coxswain, and a rebel trick test Frank before an honorable discharge closes the book. Castlemon writes a brisk boys tale of river war and young command.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardino-ca:
Bernardino Campi, an Italian painter of the Lombard school, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Cremona in 1522, he died at Reggio about 1590. His father Pietro first taught him the goldsmith's craft, but sight of Titian's drawings and tapestry designs turned the youth to painting.

Giulio Campi at Cremona and Ippolito Costa at Mantua taught him next, and by nineteen he was painting on his own, soon outstripping his masters. Deeply moved by Correggio, Titian, Raphael, and Romano, he tried to fuse their strengths into one style. The entry presents an ambitious painter chasing a perfect manner.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesarea-phil:
Caesarea Philippi, also called Caesarea Paneas, grew from a grotto shrine to the god Pan, which gave it the early Greek name Panion. Augustus gave the town to Herod in 20 B.C., and Herod built a splendid temple there in the emperor's honor. The tetrarch Philip later adorned it and named it for his protector Tiberius, hence Caesarea Philippi.

Near this city Peter made his confession of Christ, and here lived the woman healed of bleeding, who by tradition set up a bronze group showing her cure. The town early answered to Tyre as suffragan, and after the Crusaders took it about 1132 a Latin see arose. Today it is Banias, a small village below Mount Hermon, where the grotto of Pan gives rise to a main source of the Jordan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carpi:
Carpi is a diocese in the province of Modena in central Italy. The city once belonged to Countess Matilda, passing to the Holy See from 1115 to 1215. It then passed to Modena until 1319 and to the Pio family, vassals of the Holy See, until 1525. Charles V, who had held Carpi since 1525, gave it in 1530 to Alfonso I d'Este, Duke of Ferrara. Only in 1779 did Pius VI make it a see, with Francesco Benincasa as first bishop.

Its cathedral, built by King Aistulf in 756, was wholly rebuilt and richly adorned under Duke Alberto Pio. In 1855 the see became a suffragan of Modena. The diocese counts 70,000 people with 31 parishes, 50 churches and chapels, 88 priests, and four religious houses for women.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chorepiscopi:
An entry on the chorepiscopi, rural bishops of the Eastern Church whose jurisdiction covered country districts rather than cities. The earliest known is Zoticus, whom Eusebius names as bishop of the village of Cumana in Phrygia in the later second century. At first these bishops exercised every episcopal function, but from the later third century they answered to the city bishops.

Ancyra in 314 and Antioch in 341 barred them from ordaining without the bishop's written leave. Sardica in 343 ruled that no rural bishop be consecrated where a priest would do, and Laodicea in 380 ordered them replaced by periodeutai, travelling priests acting for the city bishops. The Second Council of Nicaea in 787 mentions them last in the East, though Nestorians kept them until the thirteenth century and Maronites and Jacobites keep them still. In the West they faded in the tenth and eleventh centuries before the archdeacons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filippino-lip:
Filippino Lippi was an Italian painter, son and artistic heir of Filippo Lippi. Born at Prato in 1458, he trained under Fra Diamante in Botticelli's studio. His Vision of St Bernard of 1480 charmed Florence as the most charming of altarpieces. He completed Masaccio's Brancacci chapel frescoes with marvellous suppleness and grace.

At Rome he painted St Thomas Aquinas frescoes at Santa Maria sopra Minerva. His Strozzi chapel of 1502 shows strange theatrical grace, movement, and ornament. Raphael borrowed gestures and ideas freely from his compositions. He died at Florence in 1515, gifted to his fingertips and hospitable to all beauty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filippo-lippi:
Filippo Lippi was an Italian painter born at Florence about 1406 and dead at Spoleto in 1469. Left an orphan at two, he entered a Carmelite convent at eight and took vows at sixteen. The Brancacci chapel frescoes of Masolino and Masaccio decided his vocation as a painter. Cosimo de' Medici became his great patron, locking him up at times to compel him to work.

His life was disordered: he forged to escape debts and lost a benefice for his crimes. Yet from 1452 to 1464 he painted his chief works, the Prato frescoes on John the Baptist and Stephen. The Feast of Herod and the Death of St. Stephen remain classics of their generation. His last works, at Spoleto cathedral, were finished after his death by his pupil Fra Diamante.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-galeazzo-camp:
Galeazzo Campi, an Italian painter born at Cremona in 1475, left modest work overshadowed by greater names. He is said to have studied under Boccaccino, though Lanzi doubted it, since Campi's style differs so much from his master's. He lacked great talent, and most of his painting reads as a weak echo of Perugino. He died in 1536.

His best piece is a self-portrait of 1528, honored with a place in Florence's Uffizi Gallery. More curious and celebrated is his Raising of Lazarus, painted in 1515 and owned in 1903 by Canon Bignami. A Cremona Virgin and Child also earns mention. Campi left three sons, all painters, though whether Bernardino Campi belonged to his house remains unsettled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giulio-campi:
Giulio Campi was an Italian painter and architect born at Cremona about 1500, who died there in 1572. Eldest son of Galeazzo Campi, his first teacher, he studied painting, architecture, and modelling at Mantua in 1522 under the great Romano. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the Ludovico Carracci of Cremona, though he came first.

He visited Rome and studied the antique with ardor. With the other Campi, he worked to rid painting of empty mannerisms and give it healthy vitality. At twenty-seven he painted his masterpiece for Sant' Abbondio, a Virgin and Child with Saints Celsus and Nazarus, masterly in drawing and splendid in color. His frescoes hang in the churches of Cremona, Mantua, and Milan, and Saint Margaret's in his native town amounts to a gallery of his work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mississippi:
Mississippi, one of the United States of America, takes its name from the Mississippi River forming its western boundary. The Act of Congress of 1 March 1817 creating the state fixed its bounds from the Tennessee line to the Gulf of Mexico, including islands within six leagues of the shore. The state is largely lowland, drained by the Mississippi and its tributaries, with fertile soil and a warm climate.

Its population was long rural and agricultural, cotton dominating its economy. The Diocese of Natchez covers the entire state, and in 1910 its Catholic population amounted to 25,701, including 2,017 coloured and 233 Indian Catholics. The 1890 state constitution bars testamentary bequests to religious or charitable uses, and statutes limit the property religious bodies may hold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paolo-sarpi:
Paolo Sarpi was a Servite friar and anti-papal historian and statesman, born at Venice on 14 August 1552 and dead there on 14 or 15 January 1623. Joining the Servites at thirteen, he swapped his baptismal name Pietro for Paolo. Professor of theology and canon law at twenty, he taught philosophy at Venice, was ordained in 1574, and served as provincial in 1579 and procurator general at Rome from 1585 to 1588.

Back in Venice he turned to letters. His anti-church leanings showed, fed by friendship with Protestants and hostile statesmen. Rome thrice rejected Venice's nominations of him to bishoprics, at Milopotamo, Caorle, and Nona. The more he opposed Rome, the dearer he grew to Doge Leonardo Donato. The doge made him state theological consultor at two hundred ducats a year. From that post he shaped Venice's defiance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pasquale-gall:
Pasquale Galluppi was an Italian philosopher born at Tropea in Calabria on 2 April 1770. He died at Naples on 13 December 1846, where he taught at the university from 1831. His chief works include a philosophical essay on criticism of human knowledge in four volumes. They also include letters on philosophy from Descartes to Kant, elements of philosophy, lessons in logic and metaphysics, and a philosophy of the will.

Trained in Cartesianism as tempered by Leibniz, Wolff, and Genovesi, he mixed assent and dissent toward Descartes, French and English sensists, Kant, and Reid's Scottish school. Human knowledge was his chief puzzle. He held its objective reality on consciousness's witness, which reveals both inner experience and its outer causes. Against sensists he denied the mind was merely passive, likening it to a builder ordering materials and drawing new truths sensation alone could never reach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philippi:
Philippi was a Macedonian city named for Philip, Philip of Macedon's prize from the gold country. The region began as Datos, a Thasian outpost called Crenides, lost to Thracians about 460 BC and refounded by Thasians just as gold deposits stirred the neighbours. Philip seized it in 360 BC, renamed it for himself, built a fortress barring the road between Pangaeus and Haemus, and drew over 1,000 talents a year from its mines.

Rome took it in 168 BC, and in autumn 42 BC the triumvirs beat Brutus and Cassius on its marshy plain, both republicans taking their own lives. A Roman colony followed, renamed Colonia Augusta Julia Philippensis after Actium. The entry also follows its Christian story, from Ignatius of Antioch passing through to Paul's letter to its church, whose bishops the lists preserve.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierfrancesco:
Pierfrancesco Scarampi was an Oratorian and papal envoy to Ireland, born to a noble Piedmont family in 1596. Destined for the army, he felt a religious call on a visit to Rome and entered St. Philip Neri's Oratory in 1636. In 1643, at Luke Wadding's urging, Urban VIII sent him to the Irish Confederation's Supreme Council, commending him to bishops and council as a man of noble birth, virtue, and administrative skill.

Irish Catholics welcomed him as an angel from heaven, with bishops, nobility, and cannon salutes. At Kilkenny he saw dissension as the Confederation's mortal danger and begged the council to shun compromise with religion's and country's enemies. Recalled to Rome in May 1645, he left amid tears, escorting five Irish students including the future martyr Oliver Plunkett. He died nursing plague victims at Rome's lazaretto in 1656, and Benedict XIV styled him Venerable.
confessions-of-an-inquiring-spirit-and-s:
Samuel Taylor Coleridge left his Confessions of an Inquiring Spirit as letters to a friend, and this 1892 Cassell edition adds miscellaneous essays from The Friend. Coleridge confesses that he cannot accept one doctrine: that every word of the Bible was dictated without error. Yet he holds his faith the firmer for separating the book's religion from theories about its inspiration. The letters argue gently, personally, and with a poet's care for what words can bear.

An introduction sketches his life from Ottery St. Mary through Christ's Hospital and Cambridge to his strange enlistment in the dragoons. The miscellaneous pieces show the same mind ranging over politics, poetry, and morals. It is Coleridge the thinker in short compass, questioning the letter to save the spirit.
doe-osti-3013184-fast-epitaxial-growth-a: CdZnTe got epitaxially grown, and this DOE text dopes the silicon substrate fast. The pages detail the single-crystal findings. The materials folks get their method. The growth was fast epitaxial. The method was material. The doping was extrinsic. The substrate was silicon.
doe-osti-3362852-investigation-of-u-cont: U content got swipe-investigated, and this DOE text samples J-swipe PIC. The pages detail the findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The samples were PIC. The data were nuclear. The J-swipe were investigation. The PIC were samples.
frank-on-the-lower-mississippi:
Harry Castlemon's Frank on the Lower Mississippi is a Civil War boys' story set after the fall of Vicksburg. Frank, leaning against one of his own great guns, watches war-worn soldiers march into the rebel stronghold that had so long withstood fleet and army.

Chapters follow a new paymaster, a night expedition, Archie in a predicament, a run for life, Frank turning detective, and Frank's first command. Up the Washita, rival spies, a scouting party and a rebel trick carry the action toward an honourable discharge. Castlemon writes brisk, patriotic adventure for boys, and readers who like river war stories will enjoy Frank's service afloat.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SovietUseOfAssa: A CIA memorandum dated February 17, 1964, takes up a grim Cold War subject: Soviet use of assassination and kidnapping. The catalog record gives the date, the agency, and the topic, but no summary of the memo's findings. Even so, the title alone shows what American intelligence officers were studying three months after President Kennedy's murder, when questions about state-sponsored killing carried fresh weight.
life-on-the-mississippi:
Mark Twain's complete river memoir anchors this edition. Chapter One argues the Mississippi is well worth reading about. The river empties four hundred six million tons of mud yearly, he notes. De Soto first saw it in 1542, by Twain's telling.

Early commerce, coal fleets, and timber rafts fill the next chapters. A boy's ambition to become a steamboatman drives the story forward. Village scenes and runaways crowd the apprentice years. Twain mixes river history with his own cub-pilot memories throughout. La Salle thinks he will take a hand, one chapter title jokes. Cat-fish, buffaloes, and Indian rock paintings enliven the history chapters.
podcast-dannyjones-o5AvRPCzPpI:
Psychologist Charles Morgan joins Danny Jones to warn about DARPA tech he says should not exist. Morgan has worked with the CIA on the mind under stress. The episode title bills him as a CIA psychologist with an alarm.

Morgan explains tools that can plant thoughts, read stress, or break a mind at range, as he presents them. He warns that such tech will not stay in state hands. Jones asks what laws could cage it. Listeners get a stark tour of mind tech from a man who helped test it. The library holds the talk as an archive record of his warnings.
podcast-joerogan-Ol7PofIyZPI:
Adventurer Dan Richards joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2267 with tales from Antarctic expeditions. Richards has worked and traveled in some of the coldest, emptiest places on Earth. Rogan, who loves stories of endurance, lets him set the scenes.

Richards describes the work of moving across ice, the weather that can kill a careless team, and the strange beauty that draws people back. Rogan asks about fear, failure, and the people who thrive down there. The episode is a travel story at the extreme edge of the map, told by a man who has stood where almost no listener ever will.
the-blonde-lady-being-a-record-of-the-du:
Maurice Leblanc's duel of wits between Arsene Lupin and an English detective was translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and published by Doubleday, Page in New York in 1910. Copyright entries run from 1907 to 1910. In England the book appeared as Arsene Lupin versus Holmlock Shears.

Illustrations are by H. Richard Boehm. Contents divide the book into episodes, the first named for the blonde lady of the title. A gentleman thief matched against a thinly renamed English detective is the book's plain premise. Readers can expect disguise, pursuit, and reversals as each man tries to out-think the other across linked cases.
the-shagganappi:
E. Pauline Johnson, known as Tekahionwake, wrote The Shagganappi. She dedicated it to the Boy Scouts. Ernest Thompson Seton supplied an introduction. Seton recalls his first meeting with Tekahionwake, the Indian girl. She stood as the ideal type of her race, he writes. Lithe and active, she had clean-cut aquiline features and long dark hair.

They met at a private view of one of Seton's pictures, a wolf scene. She claimed him as a Medicine Brother, he says. She herself was of the Wolf Clan of the Mohawks. Seton quotes her charge to him near the end of her life. Never let anyone call me a white woman, she said. Her aim and pride were to sing the glories of her own people, she told him.
the-unwritten-literature-of-the-hopi: Hattie Greene Lockett wrote The Unwritten Literature of the Hopi for the University of Arizona Bulletin, issued at Tucson on May 15, 1933 as Social Science Bulletin number two. This record gives the title pages and a detailed contents list, without the study's chapters. Early sections introduce the Hopi, their country, and the meaning of myth in early life. Later headings cover social organization, clan and marriage, property, divorce, and the work of women and men. Pottery and basket symbolism, house building, and Hopi myth and folktale follow.
